extracted.intended_audience: experimental scientists and students performing quantitative measurements (physicists, chemists, astronomers, metrologists)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing and carrying out quantitative experiments so as to minimise, detect, and correct measurement errors using avoidance, compensation, reversal, and averaging methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek to avoid the source of error
rubrics_metrics.description: First of all, seek to avoid the source of error altogether if it can be conveniently done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer eliminating a disturbing cause rather than compensating for it. Example: place a clock in a vacuous case to remove atmospheric-pressure effects rather than compensating mechanically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make errors small and especially constant when avoidance impossible
rubrics_metrics.description: If not possible to avoid the source, make the experiment so that the error may be as small, but more especially as constant, as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design procedures and apparatus to minimise magnitude and variability of errors so they are easier to correct or average out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine and correct error by calculation when feasible
rubrics_metrics.description: If the means are at hand for determining its amount by calculation from other experiments and principles of science, allow the error to exist and make a correction in the result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record auxiliary measurements (e.g., barometer/thermometer and object volumes for buoyancy corrections) and compute corrections rather than masking them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use counteracting (mechanical) compensation when correction impractical
rubrics_metrics.description: If correction cannot be accurately done or involves too much labour for the purposes in view, then throw in a counteracting error which shall as nearly as possible be of equal amount in all circumstances with that to be eliminated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: attach a sealed dummy globe of equal capacity when weighing gas in a glass globe to cancel air buoyancy; couple two equal magnetised needles in opposite directions in a galvanometer to null Earth's magnetism. Note: this is an intentional balancing of errors rather than analytical correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical compensation is a last resource
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanical compensation is the last resource, and in the more accurate observations it is likely to introduce more uncertainty than it removes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer analytic determination of small errors where possible. Exceptions exist where mechanical compensation gives superior stability (e.g., invariable bars for baseline measurement, compensated bars for thermal expansion, magnet+barometer compensation for pendulum clocks at Greenwich). Assess by experiment whether compensation improves accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of reversal to eliminate directional biases
rubrics_metrics.description: Make able to reverse the apparatus and mode of procedure so as to make the interfering cause act alternately in opposite directions; if we can get two experimental results, one of which is as much too great as the other is too small, the true result is the mean of the two apparent results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply reversal whenever an asymmetry in mounting/centering can produce opposite-sign errors. Examples: reverse weights on an imperfect balance and take geometric/arithmetic mean; reverse telescope/axis in transit circle observations; turn a dip needle 180° and combine readings. When reversal is applicable, the error equals half the difference; the mean reduces/eliminates that systematic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine multiple reversals/readings to remove all eliminable errors
rubrics_metrics.description: To ensure all possible accuracy each reversal ought to be combined with each other reversal, so that the needle will be observed in eight different positions by sixteen readings, the mean of the whole of which will give the required inclination free from all eliminable errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take multiple readings in all reversed configurations (e.g., read both ends, turn instrument, reverse axis/poles) and average across the full set to cancel centring, zero, axis, and pole-related errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read paired or symmetric indicators and average
rubrics_metrics.description: Read off at the same time both ends of the telescope (or both ends of a divided circle) and take the mean to reduce centring errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where instruments permit paired or symmetric readings, simultaneous or alternating paired observations produce errors equal and opposite; their mean is nearly free from those errors. Used extensively in practical astronomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use symmetric paired apparatus to cancel envelope/ambient effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ equal and similar paired enclosures (e.g., two connected glass tubes in Faraday's torsion balance) placed in similar parts of the field so that envelope and air magnetism produce opposite effects and cancel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments with matched samples so that envelope and surrounding-medium effects are the same on both and cancel when comparing (examples: oxygen vs nitrogen tubes; full vs empty globe when weighing gas). Follow up with additional controls (e.g., withdraw oxygen to compare vacuum vs nitrogen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternate reciprocal experiments to cancel environment-driven biases
rubrics_metrics.description: When a disturbing cause (e.g., wind) can be made to act in opposite directions, make reciprocal observations so that the mean of the results is free from disturbance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in long-distance sound-velocity experiments make signals from both stations simultaneously so wind accelerates one signal and retards the other, cancelling wind effect in mean. Choose calm conditions first where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of results that 'agree too closely'
rubrics_metrics.description: If results agree too closely, suspect that the apparatus is restricted in its operation or that the actual results have not been faithfully recorded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Very close agreement can indicate systematic suppression of variation (instrument limitation) or observer/recorder bias; investigate apparatus freedom and recording fidelity rather than assuming high precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the mean (average) to eliminate unknown source errors
rubrics_metrics.description: The elimination of errors of unknown sources is almost always accomplished by taking the mean (average) of several discrepant numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect multiple independent observations made in an unbiassed manner and compute the arithmetic mean to approximate the true value; this rests on probability theory (see probable mean).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish three uses/types of the mean
rubrics_metrics.description: A mean result may be: (1) a Fictitious mean or Average (representative number), (2) a Precise mean result (approximately free from disturbing quantities that act oppositely), or (3) a Probable mean result (more or less free from unknown and uncertain errors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't conflate these uses—each has different interpretation and justification. Use 'average' for fictitious representative numbers, 'mean' for approximation to a definite existing quantity when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer arithmetic mean as default, but choose mean type by problem structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Regarding the mean in the absence of express qualification to the contrary the arithmetic mean is generally understood; but there are cases where other means must be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use geometric mean for multiplicative/ratio growth rates and when true value arises from multiplicative processes (e.g., mean rate of progress, price-rises over time). Use harmonic mean where reciprocals are relevant (e.g., average of rates). When quantities differ very little arithmetic and geometric means are approximately the same and arithmetic may be used as substitute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use geometric mean when true result is multiplicative or from reversal in imperfect balances
rubrics_metrics.description: When in an imperfect balance we reverse the weights to eliminate error, the true weight will be the geometric mean of the two apparent weights. In statistics and commerce the geometric mean ought strictly to be used (e.g., average rate of progress).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: commodity price changes over periods (use geometric mean rather than arithmetic to get true average rate). For small differences arithmetic mean approximates geometric mean; otherwise use geometric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use harmonic mean for averages of reciprocals
rubrics_metrics.description: There is also the harmonic mean, which is the reciprocal of the arithmetic mean of the reciprocals of the quantities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply harmonic mean when averaging quantities that are naturally expressed as reciprocals (e.g., averaging speeds over equal distances). Provide formulae where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not confuse 'mean' and 'average' terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific men ought to mark the difference by using the word 'mean' when it denotes approximation to a definite existing quantity, and 'average' when the mean is only a fictitious quantity used for convenience of thought and expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be precise in language to avoid conceptual errors; Quetelet and Herschel emphasized this distinction. Use the terminology consistent with the intended interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use probability theory justification for probable mean
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of the mean to give a result more or less free from unknown and uncertain errors (the Probable mean) rests entirely upon the theory of probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using the mean to reduce random/unknown errors, rely on probabilistic reasoning and statistical principles (later chapters referenced). Collect sufficient independent observations for the probabilistic averaging to be effective.
